summary: AstroRelics: Voices of the Cosmos is an interactive educational storytelling platform created for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge under the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" theme. Designed for school-age space enthusiasts, the project transforms NASA’s retired and stationary hardware on the Moon and Mars—such as the Apollo Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector and the Opportunity rover—into engaging, first-person narrators.   Using React, Three.js, and NASA’s Open Data APIs, users explore an interactive 3D map of lunar and Martian landing sites. By clicking on specific hardware, students listen to immersive audio-visual "diaries" told from the equipment’s perspective, followed by interactive mini-missions that demonstrate the real-world astrophysics and scientific discoveries each tool enabled.   Our goal is to reframe discarded spacecraft not as "space junk," but as enduring monuments of human ingenuity. By combining emotional storytelling, accurate mission telemetry, and lightweight web accessibility, AstroRelics sparks lasting STEM curiosity and inspires the next generation of space explorers.
details:
• What it does & how it works: Our project, AstroRelics: Voices of the Cosmos, is an interactive web-based storytelling platform that brings NASA's left-behind space hardware on the Moon and Mars to life. Users explore a 3D map of celestial landing sites, click on iconic equipment (such as the Apollo Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector or the Opportunity rover), and experience first-person audio-visual stories narrated from the hardware's perspective, followed by interactive mini-missions demonstrating the science each tool enabled.
  • Benefits & intended impact: Designed specifically for school-age space enthusiasts, the platform transforms static historical facts into emotional, hands-on learning experiences. Our intended impact is to spark long-term curiosity in STEM, showing students that retired or stationary spacecraft are not mere "space junk," but enduring monuments of human ingenuity and ongoing scientific discovery.
  • Tools, software & technologies used: We built the front-end using HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (React), and Three.js for interactive 3D planetary mapping. We integrated NASA's Open Data Portals and NASA Image and Video Library APIs for accurate mission telemetry and photography, and used Figma and Blender for UI/UX design and low-poly 3D hardware models.
  • Creativity: Instead of a traditional encyclopedia format, we personified NASA's hardware—giving each rover, lander, and scientific instrument its own voice, personality, and "diary" entries. Blending emotional storytelling with gamified physics challenges makes complex astrophysics accessible and memorable for young learners.
  • Key factors considered: Our team prioritized age-appropriate accessibility (clear language, intuitive navigation, and visual cues for K–12 students), scientific accuracy backed by official NASA mission archives, and lightweight web performance so the platform runs smoothly on standard school computers and tablets.
